ideas: Every change is checked automatically before it reaches users
Steps: write, review, test, release in small pieces
Benefit: small, frequent, safe releases instead of big risky ones

phrases.meaning: find mistakes before they cause damage

phrases.meaning: links the idea to the listener's benefit
return to the previous working version

learn.explain: CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery (or Deployment). It is the automated path that takes code from a developer's laptop to real users. When a developer finishes a change, they open a pull request. Another engineer reviews it, and at the same time automated tests run to check that nothing is broken: that's continuous integration. If everything passes, the change is merged and the pipeline builds the app and releases it, often first to a test environment, then to a small group of users, then to everyone: that's continuous delivery. Because each change is small and checked automatically, teams can release many times a day with less risk, and if something goes wrong they can quickly go back to the previous version.
points: Every change goes through the same automatic checks; no manual copying of files.
Small, frequent releases are safer than one big release every few months.
If something breaks, rolling back to the last good version takes minutes.
learn.analogy: Think of it like a car factory production line. Every car passes the same quality checks at every station, automatically, before it leaves the factory. If one station finds a problem, the line stops and that car never reaches a customer.

mistakes: Describing the tool (GitHub Actions, Jenkins) instead of the process.
Forgetting why it matters to the business: speed and safety together.
Saying "tests mean no bugs". Tests reduce risk; they don't remove it.

model: Every change our developers make goes through the same path, step by step, before it reaches your users. First, the developer finishes a small change on their laptop and asks a colleague to review it. While the colleague reads it, a set of automatic tests runs, checking that nothing that worked yesterday is broken today. If the review and the tests pass, the change is released, first to a test copy of the system, then to a small group of users, and finally to everyone. Think of it like a production line in a car factory. Every car passes the same quality checks at every station, and if one station finds a problem, the line stops and that car never leaves the factory. The automatic tests are our safety net: they catch problems early. What this means for you is two things. First, speed: we release in small batches, several times a week, so the improvements you ask for arrive in days, not months. Second, safety: because each change is small, if something does go wrong after it goes live, we can roll back to the last working version in a few minutes.
short: Every change goes through the same automatic path: a colleague reviews it, tests check nothing is broken, and only then does it reach your users, first a small group, then everyone. What this means for you is speed and safety together: improvements arrive in days, and if something goes wrong, we roll back in minutes.

audience.engineer: Our flow is trunk-based. You branch, open a PR, and the pipeline in GitHub Actions runs lint, unit tests and integration tests against a Postgres container, usually in about eight minutes. One approval plus a green build lets you merge. Merging to main builds a Docker image, deploys it to staging, and runs smoke tests. Production deploys are a canary: five percent of traffic for fifteen minutes while we watch error rate and latency, then a full rollout. Rollback is just redeploying the previous image tag. Feature flags let us merge unfinished work safely, so please wrap anything user-facing in a flag.

followUps.q: Can we test new features before our users see them?
followUps.answer: Yes. We can switch a new feature on just for your team first. You try it in the real system, give us feedback, and only then do we turn it on for everyone.

followUps.q: What if a bug still gets through?
followUps.answer: It can happen; tests reduce risk, they don't remove it. That's why we release to a small group first and watch closely. If we see a problem, we roll back in minutes, then fix it properly.

followUps.q: Why can't you release on Friday afternoon?
followUps.answer: We technically can, but we usually avoid it. If something goes wrong on Friday evening, fewer people are around to fix it. It's a small habit that protects your weekend and ours.
